sentences: This is The Sleeping Gypsy by Henri Rousseau.
Across a canvas two metres wide stretches a moonlit, arid desert under a deep blue sky.
On it, very quietly, appear a sleeping woman and a single lion, and nothing else moves.
Rousseau worked collecting taxes on goods entering Paris, which earned him the nickname Le Douanier, the customs officer.
He took up painting seriously in his early forties and retired early in 1893 to paint full time.
The lion, its tail raised high, is drawn with simple outlines and broad blocks of colour.
Critics at first mocked this self-taught painter's plain manner, yet it is exactly what gives the scene its still, dreamlike strangeness.
Now follow the lion's body to its head.
The maned lion lowers its head toward the sleeper.
With wide, watchful eyes, it cautiously sniffs at her, as if trying to understand who she is.
In the upper right hangs a full moon with an almost human face, and a few stars glitter in the deep blue sky.
Rousseau himself said the picture had a very poetic moonlight effect, and the cool light falls evenly over everything.
Under the moon, the woman sleeps deeply, still holding her staff.
Rousseau described her as a wandering mandolin player overcome by fatigue, and a lion that picks up her scent yet does not devour her.
Her robe and the blanket beneath her are covered in rainbow stripes.
Against the cool night landscape, these warm bands of colour anchor the whole composition, bending gently with the folds of the cloth.
Beside her, within easy reach, lie a mandolin and a tall water jar with a slender neck.
Music, water and a traveller's few belongings are enough to hint at her long journey.
Even the mandolin's strings are carefully drawn.
He first showed the picture at the Salon des Indépendants in 1897 and tried, without success, to sell it to the mayor of his hometown, Laval.
It then sat for years in the collection of a Paris charcoal merchant.
It resurfaced in 1924, when the critic Louis Vauxcelles came across it, and in 1939 it was given to the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
Rousseau's work went on to influence Picasso and the Surrealists.
Step back, and everything seems to hold its breath, without a breath of wind anywhere.
Is this the woman's dream, or one we are dreaming ourselves?
Stay for a moment inside that stillness before moving on.
